meaning: Boldly doing something without being put off by difficulty, danger, or obstacles. It carries a tone of praise.
connection: Noun + をものともせず（に）

senses.label: In defiance of hardship
senses.meaning: Facing difficulty, danger, or harsh conditions without flinching and pushing on. Like “undaunted by ...” or “in defiance of ...”. Mostly used to praise someone else's courage or perseverance.
senses.connection: Noun + をものともせず（に）. Common nouns: 「困難」, 「危険」, 「悪天候」, 「けが」, 「批判」, 「逆境」
examples: Undaunted by his injured leg, he ran all the way to the finish.
The rescue team headed into the mountains in defiance of the violent storm.
Brushing off the objections of those around her, she started her own business.

notes: Normally not used about yourself, since it sounds like boasting: ✕「私は熱をものともせず出勤した」→ ○「熱を押して出勤した」「熱があったが出勤した」.
The first part must be an objective obstacle such as hardship or danger, not another person's feelings: ✕「親の心配をものともせず遊びに行った」→ ○「親の心配をよそに遊びに行った」.
The second part describes something that actually happened. It cannot be a command, invitation, or statement of intent: ✕「困難をものともせずに頑張れ」→ ○「困難に負けずに頑張れ」.
It carries a tone of praise, so do not use it for reckless rule-breaking such as running a red light; that would sound like admiring bad behavior. For criticism, use 「信号もかまわず渡った」.

daily.title: Watching sports news
daily.description: Reading a report about an athlete who played while injured.
daily.example: Undaunted by a broken bone, the player took the field.

daily.title: Telling a friend what you saw
daily.description: Praising an elderly neighbor's perseverance.
daily.example: The old lady next door goes for a walk every morning, rain or shine.

work.title: Business coverage
work.description: A report describing how a company overcame hard times.
work.example: Undaunted by the recession, the company keeps growing its sales.

etymology: Made of 「もの（物）とも＋せず」. 「〜をものとする」 means “to treat ... as something that matters”. Adding the negative 「せず」 gives “not even treating it as anything”, that is, “thinking nothing of it”.

similar.title: 〜を押して
similar.explanation: 〜を押して also means “in spite of…”, but the first part is usually your own illness or someone's objections, so it is natural to use about yourself (「病を押して出席した」). 〜をものともせず stresses “paying no heed at all” and carries an onlooker's praise, so it is not normally used about yourself.

similar.title: 〜を顧みず／〜も顧みず
similar.explanation: 〜を顧みず means “disregarding (one's own safety, family, etc.)”, stressing that the person acts knowing the cost, and is typical of self-sacrificing scenes (「危険を顧みず救助した」). 〜をものともせず stresses overcoming obstacles and pressing forward; the focus is on being undaunted.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: 〜もかまわず means “not caring about (other people's eyes, the setting, rules)” and tends to carry negative judgment (「人目もかまわず泣いた」). With 〜をものともせず, the first part is hardship or danger, and the tone is praise.

similar.title: 〜をよそに
similar.explanation: 〜をよそに also means “ignoring”, but its object is other people's feelings such as worry, expectations, or objections, and it is often critical (「親の心配をよそに」). 〜をものともせず takes hardship or danger as its object and is praising.

formation: Built from 「もの（物）」 + the emphatic particle 「とも」 + 「せず」 (the classical negative of 「する」). The original sense of 「〜をものとする」 is “to take something as a matter of consequence”; 「とも」 intensifies it to “not even…”, and negating it with 「せず」 gives “not even treating it as a real concern.” Because of this, the first part is always an obstacle that would normally make people back off: hardship, injury, opposition. And since the subject carries on regardless, the second part is a positive action that is actually carried out, which gives the whole phrase its tone of praise and admiration. 「せず」 is the classical negative form, which also explains the formal, written feel.

meaning: Being forced by outside circumstances to take some action, with no other choice. 「させる」 means forcing someone else to do so.
connection: Noun + を余儀なくされる／を余儀なくさせる

senses.label: Be forced to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜を余儀なくされる」 means having to do something because of a cause you can't resist, such as a natural disaster, an accident, or the economy. Like “be forced to ...” or “have no choice but to ...”. The subject is the one affected.
senses.connection: Action noun + を余儀なくされる. Common nouns: 「中止」, 「延期」, 「変更」, 「撤退」, 「入院」, 「避難」
examples: Because of the typhoon, the game had to be canceled.
Residents have been forced to live as evacuees for a long time.
Due to falling profits, the factory was forced to close.

senses.label: Force someone to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜を余儀なくさせる」 means something forces other people to take an action. The subject is usually the cause (an event or situation).
senses.connection: Cause + が + person + に + noun + を余儀なくさせる
examples: The heavy snow left many cars stranded.
A string of scandals forced the company president to resign.

notes: Mixing up the passive and the causative reverses the meaning. The subject of 「される」 is the person forced (「選手は引退を余儀なくされた」); the subject of 「させる」 is the cause (「けがが選手に引退を余儀なくさせた」). ✕「選手は引退を余儀なくさせた」.
It takes only nouns, not verbs: ✕「帰るを余儀なくされた」→ ○「帰国を余儀なくされた」.

It implies “against one's own will, forced by outside pressure.” If you resigned voluntarily and say 「退職を余儀なくされました」, people may take it as hinting that the company pushed you out, which can cause misunderstandings at work.
Used for trivial everyday matters it sounds exaggerated and stiff: ✕ to a friend 「残業を余儀なくされた」→ in speech, 「残業するしかなかった」「残業せざるを得なかった」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report about the effects of a disaster.
daily.example: The earthquake forced many people to evacuate.

daily.title: Talking about your own experience
daily.description: Describing a hospital stay in a fairly formal setting.
daily.example: Last year, illness forced me into a long hospital stay.

work.title: Business notice
work.description: A company explains to customers that a plan had to change.
work.example: Due to a parts shortage, we have been forced to postpone the release date.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: A report on companies struggling to stay in business.
work.example: The weak yen is forcing many companies to raise prices.

etymology: 「余儀」 is a word from Chinese meaning “another way, another option”. 「余儀ない」 is “there is no other way”, and 「余儀なくされる」 is “being left with no other way”, that is, “being forced”.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: 〜ざるを得ない follows a verb and expresses the speaker's own judgment, after weighing things, that there is “no choice but to…” (「中止せざるを得ない」). 〜を余儀なくされる follows a noun and stresses that one is objectively forced by external causes; it is more formal and sounds like a news report.

similar.title: 〜ほかない・〜よりほかない
similar.explanation: 〜ほかない means “have no choice but to…” and works in both speech and writing, stressing resignation at having no other way. 〜を余儀なくされる is a formal, objective written expression that stresses being forced by outside pressure.

similar.title: 〜羽目になる
similar.explanation: 〜羽目になる is colloquial and means ending up in an unpleasant situation for some reason, often with self-mockery (「徹夜する羽目になった」). 〜を余儀なくされる is an objective, formal written expression with no personal feeling.

formation: 「余儀」 (another way) + 「ない」 forms the adjective 「余儀ない」 (“there is no alternative”). Its adverbial form 「余儀なく」 combines with 「する」 into 「〜を余儀なくする」, meaning “to make something a thing with no alternative.” Adding the passive 「される」 makes the subject the party left with no choice, giving “be forced to…”; adding the causative 「させる」 makes the subject the cause that leaves people no choice, giving “force (someone) to…”. Since 「を」 marks what one is forced to do, only nouns can precede it (mostly Sino-Japanese action nouns such as 「中止」 or 「撤退」). The passive/causative difference decides whether the subject is the affected party or the cause.

meaning: Ignoring other people's worry, hopes, criticism, etc. and doing as one pleases. Often carries the speaker's criticism or feelings about it.

senses.label: Ignoring others
senses.meaning: Paying no attention to the worry, hopes, or objections of people involved, and going ahead anyway. Like “regardless of ...” or “ignoring ...”. Often sounds critical or resigned.
senses.connection: Noun + をよそに. Common nouns: 「心配」, 「期待」, 「反対」, 「批判」, 「忠告」
examples: Ignoring his parents' worry, the son goes out partying late every night.
Despite the residents' opposition, construction began.

senses.label: Unaffected by ...
senses.meaning: Some situation is going on nearby, but the subject has nothing to do with it and isn't affected at all. Like “in contrast to ...” or “untouched by ...”. Often paints a sharp contrast.
senses.connection: Noun + をよそに. Common nouns: 「騒ぎ」, 「喧騒」, 「不景気」, 「混乱」
examples: In contrast to the bustle of the streets, the temple grounds were completely silent.
Untouched by the recession, this shop is always full of customers.

notes: The first part cannot be the speaker's own feelings: ✕「私の心配をよそに」→ ○「親の心配をよそに」「周囲の期待をよそに」.
The subject is the one doing the ignoring; do not reverse it. 「息子は親の心配をよそに遊んでいる」 means the son ignores his parents' worry, not the other way around.
Do not use it to praise someone for not fearing hardship: ✕「激しい嵐をよそに救助に向かった」→ ○「激しい嵐をものともせず救助に向かった」.
It is mostly critical. Using it about a superior or client (「部長は皆の反対をよそに…」) amounts to saying they act high-handedly, which is rude if said to their face.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A mother complains to a friend that her child won't listen.
daily.example: Paying no attention to my worrying, my daughter went off traveling alone.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: Reading a report about a new policy.
daily.example: The bill was passed despite public criticism.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: A report notes a company growing against the trend.
work.example: Despite the slump across the industry, the company posted record profits.

etymology: 「よそ」 (written 「余所」) means “somewhere else, a place that has nothing to do with you”. 「〜をよそに（する）」 is “treating ... as someone else's business”, which led to “ignoring, paying no attention to”.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: 〜もかまわず also means “regardless of,” but usually follows other people's gaze, the setting, or rules (「人目もかまわず」) and stresses inappropriate behavior. 〜をよそに usually follows other people's feelings, attitudes, or the surrounding situation and stresses ignoring how others feel.

similar.title: 〜をものともせず
similar.explanation: 〜をものともせず takes hardship or danger as its object, means “undaunted by,” and praises. 〜をよそに takes other people's worry, expectations, etc., and is often critical or wistful.

similar.title: 〜はそっちのけで
similar.explanation: 〜はそっちのけで means setting aside something one should be doing in order to do something else (「勉強はそっちのけで遊ぶ」). 〜をよそに stresses disregarding other people's feelings or the surrounding situation.

formation: 「よそ（余所）」 means “somewhere else, a place unconnected with oneself,” and 「〜をよそに」 can be understood as a shortening of 「〜をよそにする」 (to treat something as someone else's business). The first part is something closely tied to the subject that they should care about (other people's worry, expectations, opposition, or the surrounding situation), yet it is set “elsewhere.” The result is either that the subject ignores it and does as they please (first sense), or that the subject is unaffected by it (second sense). Because it is something they ought to care about but do not, the sentence often carries criticism or a note of wonder.

meaning: Doing whatever it takes to reach a goal. Stronger and more formal than 「〜ために」.
connection: Verb nai-form + んがため（に）／んがための + noun (する → せんがため)

senses.label: Strong purpose
senses.meaning: Doing something with fierce determination to reach a goal. Like “in order to ... (at any cost)”. Mostly written, with a solemn, stiff tone.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + んがため（に）. 「する」 → 「せんがため」. Common: 「勝たんがため」, 「生きんがため」, 「売らんがため」
examples: Determined to win, they kept up grueling practice every day.
Just to stay alive, he took any job he could get.
To get at the truth, the reporter carried out interview after interview.

senses.label: ... for the sake of ...
senses.meaning: 「〜んがための + noun」 modifies a noun: “... meant only to ...”. 「売らんがための」 is often negative, suggesting “only out to make money”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + んがための + noun
examples: That's nothing but advertising meant to sell.

notes: The 「ん」 is not a negative: 「勝たんがため」 means “in order to win.” Do not misread it as the Kansai-style 「勝たん」 (“won't win”) and take it as “in order not to win.”
It attaches to the irrealis stem, not the dictionary form or the ます stem: ✕「勝つんがため」「勝ちんがため」→ ○「勝たんがため」; 「する」 becomes 「せんがため」.
Phrases like 「売らんがため」「目立たんがため」 often carry a negative sense of “only caring about X, by any means,” so using them to judge a client or partner sounds rude.
Use it only for serious goals; for trivial daily matters it is comical: ✕「パンを買わんがためにコンビニへ行く」→ ○「パンを買いにコンビニへ行く」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the hero working desperately for revenge.
daily.example: He spent ten long years in order to get his revenge.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: An essay criticizing commercial advertising.
daily.example: I have doubts about excessive advertising that's only out to sell.

work.title: Speech
work.description: The company president rallies all employees at a general meeting.
work.example: To overcome this crisis, let's all pull together as one company.

etymology: 「ん」 comes from the Classical auxiliary 「む」 (will, conjecture). 「が」 is an old case particle (like 「の」), and 「ため」 means “for the sake of”. Literally: “for the purpose of wanting to do ...”.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 〜ために is the most general way to express purpose, used in speech and writing. 〜んがため also expresses purpose with 「ため」, but the classical volitional 「ん」 adds a strong determination to do anything necessary; it is a stiff written form.

similar.title: 〜べく
similar.explanation: 〜べく is also a written “in order to…,” solemn but milder (「真相を究明すべく調査を進める」). 〜んがため shows stronger, more exaggerated determination and sometimes carries a negative “by any means” tone.

similar.title: 〜んとする
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「ん」 in both comes from the classical auxiliary 「む」. 〜んとする means “be about to… / try to…” and describes an action about to occur; 〜んがため adds 「が＋ため」 and expresses purpose.

formation: Built from the irrealis stem of a verb (the ない form minus 「ない」) + the classical volitional auxiliary 「む」 (which became 「ん」) + the classical case particle 「が」 (equivalent to modern 「の」) + 「ため（為）」. 「む」 expresses will, “want to…, intend to…,” so 「勝たんがため」 literally means “for the purpose of ‘intending to win’.” It adds a layer of subjective will beyond plain 「勝つため」, which makes it sound resolute and ready to pay any price. The 「が」 is a classical adnominal use, so the whole pattern has a strongly literary flavor. Before a noun, 「ため」 is followed by 「の」, giving 「〜んがための＋noun」. A single-minded will like 「売らんがため」 is easily read as “by any means,” which is where the negative tone comes from.

meaning: Looking as if something is just about to happen. A dramatic way to describe how extreme something is. It doesn't actually happen.
connection: Verb nai-form + んばかりに／んばかりの／んばかりだ (する → せんばかり)

senses.label: As if about to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜んばかりに」 modifies the following action: “as if about to ...”, “practically ...”. It's an exaggerated comparison. The action doesn't really happen.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + んばかりに. Common: 「泣かんばかりに」, 「飛び上がらんばかりに」, 「頭を床にこすりつけんばかりに」
examples: When she learned she'd passed, she was so happy she practically jumped for joy.
He begged as if he were about to burst into tears.

senses.label: ... that seems about to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜んばかりの + noun」 modifies a noun to show how extreme something is. Set phrases include 「あふれんばかりの」, 「割れんばかりの」, and 「輝かんばかりの」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + んばかりの + noun
examples: The hall was filled with thunderous applause.
The children flashed beaming smiles.

senses.label: Almost about to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜んばかりだ」 works as a predicate: a state is so extreme that something seems about to happen.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + んばかりだ
examples: The cherry blossoms are so full they look ready to spill over.

notes: The 「ん」 is not a negative: 「泣かんばかり」 means “almost crying,” not “not crying.”
The action in the first part has not actually happened, so you cannot use something that already did: ✕「彼は泣かんばかりに涙を流した」→ ○「彼は泣かんばかりに頼み込んだ」.
It attaches to the irrealis stem: ✕「割れるんばかりの拍手」→ ○「割れんばかりの拍手」; 「する」 becomes 「せんばかり」.
It is generally used to describe other people or things; for your own feelings 「飛び上がるほど嬉しかった」 sounds more natural.

daily.title: Describing a friend's reaction
daily.description: Telling someone how a friend reacted to a present.
daily.example: She saw the present and was so happy she nearly cried.

daily.title: At a concert
daily.description: Describing the excitement at a concert.
daily.example: When the singer came on stage, a deafening cheer went up.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report describing the moment a team wins.
work.example: When the championship was decided, the coach hugged the players, close to tears.

etymology: 「ん」 comes from the Classical auxiliary 「む」 (conjecture, will), and 「ばかり」 shows degree. Literally: “to the point of being about to ...”.

similar.title: 〜とばかりに／〜と言わんばかりに
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ばかり」 to mean “to the point of almost…”. 〜とばかりに follows a quoted phrase or inner voice and means “as if saying…” (「出て行けとばかりに」); 〜んばかりに follows the irrealis stem of a verb and means “almost doing…”.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: 〜かのようだ is an ordinary comparison, “as if…”, and the facts can be the opposite (「春が来たかのような暖かさ」). 〜んばかり stresses that the degree is so great the action is nearly performed; it is more literary and more exaggerated.

similar.title: 〜んとする
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「ん」 in both comes from the classical auxiliary 「む」. 〜んとする means “be about to…” and describes an action about to occur (「日が沈まんとしている」); 〜んばかり is an exaggerated figure of speech in which the action does not actually happen.

formation: Built from the irrealis stem of a verb + the classical auxiliary 「む」 (which became 「ん」, expressing conjecture, “will…”) + the adverbial particle 「ばかり」 (expressing extent, “to the point of…”). 「泣かんばかり」 literally means “to the extent of ‘about to cry’.” Because it uses the “about to” sense, the action does not actually happen; it only comes close, which is the source of “almost…” and “as if to…”. Followed by 「に」 it modifies an action as an adverb, with 「の」 it modifies a noun, and with 「だ」 it serves as the predicate; these three are just different ways of attaching 「ばかり」.

meaning: Someone of status or position, of all people, does something unfitting for that role. Shows the speaker's surprise, disappointment, or blame.
connection: Noun (status/position) + ともあろう + noun (人・者・方・もの)

senses.label: ... of all people
senses.meaning: Follows a role with social standing or one that deserves respect: “someone who is a ..., of all people, would ...”. The second half is usually improper behavior that doesn't fit the role, with surprise, disappointment, or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun + ともあろう + 人／者／方／もの + が. Common nouns: 「教師」, 「警察官」, 「大臣」, 「大企業」
examples: It's unforgivable for a teacher, of all people, to use violence against a student.
Imagine a police officer, of all people, driving drunk.
A minister shouldn't make such careless remarks.

notes: It is used only for conduct unbecoming of one's status, never for praise: ✕「医者ともあろう人が、患者の命を救った」→ ○「さすが医者だ」.
The rebuke is very strong. Saying 「部長ともあろう方が…」 to a superior or client amounts to publicly accusing them of failing in their duty, which is extremely rude.
It must be followed by a noun such as 「者・人・方」 before the rest of the sentence; it cannot be followed directly by a verb: ✕「教師ともあろう暴力をふるう」→ ○「教師ともあろう者が暴力をふるう」.
Do not confuse it with 「こともあろうに」 (“of all things”): the latter takes no status noun, as in 「こともあろうに社長の前で寝てしまった」.

daily.title: Reading local news
daily.description: Commenting to family after a scandal involving a public official.
daily.example: I can't believe the mayor, of all people, used tax money for himself.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: Complaining about a celebrity's bad behavior.
daily.example: It's awful for a doctor, of all people, to leak a patient's secrets.

work.title: Editorial
work.description: A newspaper editorial criticizes a big company's misconduct.
work.example: A major bank, of all institutions, leaking customer data bears heavy responsibility.

etymology: Made of the emphatic 「とも」 plus 「あろう」, the conjectural form of 「ある」. Before a noun, 「あろう」 suggests “one who rightly ought to be ...”, so the whole means “a person worthy of the name ...”.

similar.title: 〜ともなると／〜ともなれば
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「とも」 to single out a status or stage. 〜ともなると means “once one reaches the status or stage of…, naturally…” and is a neutral, objective judgment (「部長ともなると忙しい」); 〜ともあろう stresses “someone as distinguished as… and yet…” and is used only to rebuke.

similar.title: 〜まじき
similar.explanation: 〜まじき means “(conduct) unbecoming of one as…” and often pairs with 〜ともあろう: 「教師ともあろう者が、教師にあるまじき行為をした」. 〜まじき evaluates the conduct itself, while 〜ともあろう stresses the gap between status and conduct.

similar.title: 〜たる
similar.explanation: 〜たる means “as a… (one should…)” and is mostly used to state duties one ought to fulfill (「教師たる者、生徒の手本であるべきだ」). 〜ともあろう is mostly used to rebuke improper conduct that has already happened.

formation: Built from the case particle 「と」 + the emphatic particle 「も」 (「とも」: “being such a…”) + 「あろう」, the conjectural form of 「ある」. Used as a modifier, 「あろう」 gives a sense of “who ought to be so, who deserves to be called…”, so 「教師ともあろう者」 means “a person worthy of the name of teacher.” The sentence first raises the person's status to a level where fitting character is expected, then attaches conduct that does not fit; this gap creates the surprise and rebuke of “someone as distinguished as… yet actually…”. So the first part must be a status society expects much of, and a noun such as 「者・人・方・もの」 has to follow.

meaning: If you let a certain person say it. Shows a view from that person's own particular standpoint.
connection: Noun (person) + に言わせれば／に言わせると／に言わせたら

senses.label: In ...'s opinion
senses.meaning: “If you ask ...”, “in ...'s view”. It stresses that this is that person's own view, which may differ from the general one. Often used to introduce strong opinions, your own or someone else's.
senses.connection: Person noun + に言わせれば／に言わせると／に言わせたら. Common: 「私に言わせれば」, 「専門家に言わせると」
examples: If you ask me, that movie isn't interesting at all.
According to my father, young people these days lack patience.
Experts say an earthquake this size isn't unusual.

notes: 「私に言わせれば」 is forceful and implies “the rest of you don't understand,” so it can sound arrogant toward a superior or client; in formal settings say 「私見ですが」 or 「私としては」.
The word before it must be a person or organization, not a document or thing: ✕「データに言わせれば」→ ○「データによると」.
Do not use it to relay objective information such as news or weather forecasts: ✕「天気予報に言わせれば、明日は雨だ」→ ○「天気予報によると、明日は雨だ」.
The particle must be 「に」: ✕「専門家が言わせれば」→ ○「専門家に言わせれば」.

daily.title: Debating with a friend
daily.description: Disagreeing with a friend's view.
daily.example: If you ask me, that's just being selfish.

daily.title: Passing on a family member's view
daily.description: Telling a friend what your mother thinks.
daily.example: According to my mom, this shop's cakes are the best.

work.title: Meeting
work.description: Quoting a veteran colleague in a meeting.
work.example: According to our veteran staff, this plan isn't realistic.

etymology: Made of 「言わせる」, the causative of 「言う」, plus the conditional 「れば」. Literally “if you let (someone) say it”, which came to mean “in (someone's) view”.

similar.title: 〜にしたら・〜にすれば
similar.explanation: 〜にしたら is the speaker putting themselves in someone's position and guessing their feelings (「親にしたら心配だろう」). 〜に言わせれば is a claim or evaluation that the person would state outright.

similar.title: 〜からいうと・〜からいえば
similar.explanation: 〜からいうと follows nouns for a standpoint, viewpoint, or angle (「専門家の立場からいうと」) and gives the basis for a judgment. 〜に言わせれば follows a person directly and stresses that person's distinctive, subjective view.

similar.title: 〜によると・〜によれば
similar.explanation: 〜によると marks an objective source of information, and what follows is usually hearsay with 「〜そうだ」 (「ニュースによると」). 〜に言わせれば stresses that person's own opinion, which often differs from the general view.

formation: Built from a person + 「に」 (the causee of the causative) + 「言わせる」 (the causative of 「言う」) + the conditional 「れば」, literally “if (someone) were made to say.” The chance to speak is “handed over” to that person, so what follows is marked as “that person's own view,” with the implication that it differs from the general view or other people's opinions. Because it means “letting someone speak,” only a person or organization capable of voicing an opinion can come before 「に」. 「私に言わせれば」 means “if you let me say so,” and carries a strong assertion of “I see it differently.”

meaning: Being so busy with one thing that you neglect other things you should do. Often used for excuses or self-reflection.

senses.label: Too caught up in ... to ...
senses.meaning: Being wrapped up in one thing, and as a result putting off or neglecting other things you should do. Like “too busy with ... to ...”. The second half is usually a negative result.
senses.connection: Noun + にかまけて + something neglected or not done. Common nouns: 「仕事」, 「忙しさ」, 「遊び」, 「育児」
examples: Caught up in work, I neglected time with my family.
I've been so busy that I haven't contacted my friends in a while.
I was so busy having fun that I didn't study at all.

notes: The word before 「に」 is what one is immersed in, not what gets neglected. To say “absorbed in work, neglecting family,” ✕「家族にかまけて仕事をしない」→ ○「仕事にかまけて家族をおろそかにする」.
The second part must be negative: something neglected or left undone. ✕「仕事にかまけて昇進した」→ ○「仕事に打ち込んで昇進した」.
「忙しさにかまけてご無沙汰しております」 is a proper way to apologize to someone for not keeping in touch; but used to comment on a superior (「部長は仕事にかまけて…」) it becomes criticism and is rude.
Do not confuse it with the similar-looking 「にかこつけて」 (“using as a pretext”): 「出張にかこつけて観光する」 means sightseeing under the pretext of a business trip.

daily.title: Writing an apology letter
daily.description: The opening of a letter to a teacher you haven't contacted in a long time.
daily.example: I've been so caught up in my busy days that I've been terribly out of touch.

daily.title: Self-reflection
daily.description: Lamenting how long it's been since you cleaned while tidying your room.
daily.example: I was so absorbed in my hobbies that I kept skipping cleaning my room.

work.title: Work review
work.description: Reflecting on your own oversight at a review meeting.
work.example: I was so focused on immediate tasks that I didn't make a long-term plan.

etymology: 「かまける」 is an old verb that originally meant “to be tied up with something, to be absorbed only in it”. One theory links it to 「構う（かまう）」. It's usually used in the form 「〜にかまけて」.

similar.title: 〜はそっちのけで
similar.explanation: 〜はそっちのけで follows what is cast aside, while 〜にかまけて follows what one is absorbed in. They point in opposite directions but describe the same situation: 「勉強はそっちのけで遊ぶ」≈「遊びにかまけて勉強しない」.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 〜てばかりいる also means “doing nothing but…”, but merely describes constantly doing something without necessarily mentioning what is neglected (「遊んでばかりいる」). 〜にかまけて must bring out the neglected second part and is often used for self-reproach or excuses.

formation: Built from a noun + the case particle 「に」 + the te-form of the verb 「かまける」. 「かまける」 means “be tied up with something, be wholly occupied with it”; 「に」 marks what ties one up, and 「て」 links the next clause, forming the causal chain “tied up with A → so no time for B.” Since being tied up inherently means having no attention for anything else, the second part naturally describes neglect or leaving necessary things undone. And because A is presented as something that ‘holds one captive,’ the sentence carries a tone of excuse or self-reproach, using A as the reason.

meaning: Something has gone too far, beyond what can be tolerated. Strongly critical or reproachful.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem / i-adjective dictionary form / verb dictionary form + にもほどがある

senses.label: That's going too far
senses.meaning: “There's a limit to ...”, “That's way too ...”. The speaker is annoyed, indignant, or shocked by someone's words, actions, or state. Mostly used in speech for criticism or complaints.
senses.connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + にもほどがある (「冗談にも」, 「失礼にも」, 「わがままにも」); i-adjective / verb dictionary form + にもほどがある (「甘いにも」, 「ふざけるにも」)
examples: There's a limit to joking.
Breaking a promise three times? That's beyond careless.
You can't even solve this problem? That's way too dumb.

notes: It is a strong accusation and very rude to use toward a superior, client, or elder; even half-jokingly, 「失礼にもほどがある」 can cause a quarrel.
Nouns and na-adjectives take 「にも」 directly, without 「な」 or 「だ」: ✕「失礼なにもほどがある」→ ○「失礼にもほどがある」.
In formal writing it is used only for negative judgments; online, 「かわいいにもほどがある」 is a playful exaggeration, not for formal settings or for elders.

daily.title: Getting angry at a friend
daily.description: A friend makes a joke that goes too far.
daily.example: Laughing at someone's failure? That's beyond rude.

daily.title: Complaining about prices
daily.description: Seeing outrageous prices near a tourist spot.
daily.example: 2,000 yen for a cup of coffee? What a rip-off.

work.title: Venting in private
work.description: Coworkers complain about a client's unreasonable demand.
work.example: Fix everything by tomorrow? That's just absurd, isn't it?

etymology: 「ほど（程）」 means “degree, measure, limit”. Literally 「〜にもほどがある」 is “even ... has its limits”, which came to mean “that's going too far”.

similar.title: 〜すぎる
similar.explanation: 〜すぎる merely states objectively that something is “too much” (「辛すぎる」), without necessarily blaming. 〜にもほどがある carries strong dissatisfaction, blame, and indignation.

similar.title: 〜極まる／〜極まりない
similar.explanation: 〜極まりない is a written form meaning “extremely…” (「失礼極まりない」), mostly used in formal criticism. 〜にもほどがある is more colloquial and emotional, stressing that “it has gone beyond the limit.”

similar.title: 〜といったらない
similar.explanation: 〜といったらない means “so… it's beyond description,” and works for both positive and negative things (「嬉しいといったらない」). 〜にもほどがある is used only for negative criticism.

formation: Built from 「に」 (as for…) + 「も」 (even…) + 「ほど（程）」 (measure, limit) + 「がある」, literally “even A has its limits.” Appealing to the common-sense idea that everything has a limit, the speaker implies the other party has crossed it, so what is actually expressed is “that's way too much A.” Because it accuses someone of going over the line, the first part is mostly a word that already carries a negative evaluation (「冗談」「失礼」「わがまま」「ばか」), and the whole is used for criticism and indignation.

meaning: If it were ..., that would be another matter, but ... is not OK. The first part is an exception; the second part is what the speaker wants to stress.
connection: Noun + ならいざしらず／はいざしらず; verb/adjective plain form + ならいざしらず

senses.label: ... would be one thing, but
senses.meaning: “If it were ..., that would be different (understandable), but ...”. The first part names a special, extreme, or forgivable case; the second stresses that the current case can't be excused. The second half often shows surprise, dissatisfaction, or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun + ならいざしらず. Common: 「子どもならいざしらず」, 「神様ならいざしらず」, 「昔ならいざしらず」
examples: A child would be one thing, but it's embarrassing for an adult not to know this.
If it were your first time, maybe, but this is the third time, so no mistakes allowed.

senses.label: Leaving ... aside
senses.meaning: 「〜はいざしらず」 works the same way. It's often used for contrasts like “the past / others / elsewhere aside, now / we / here ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + はいざしらず. Common: 「昔はいざしらず」, 「ほかの人はいざ知らず」
examples: Whatever it was like in the past, today anyone can easily travel abroad.
I don't know about others, but I absolutely can't agree.

notes: Do not reverse the two parts: the first is the “understandable exception,” and the second is what is being criticized. ✕「大人ならいざ知らず、子どもがこんなことも知らないなんて」→ ○「子どもならいざ知らず、大人がこんなことも知らないなんて」.
The second part is mostly criticism, dissatisfaction, or a strong assertion by the speaker, not a plain objective description.
The critical tone is obvious: saying 「新人ならいざ知らず、課長が…」 to a superior is a public accusation and very rude; in speech, 「〜ならともかく」 is usually used instead.

daily.title: Criticizing bad manners
daily.description: Seeing university students being loud on the train.
daily.example: Elementary schoolers would be one thing, but university students making noise on the train is disgraceful.

daily.title: Talking about changing times
daily.description: Chatting with an older relative about changing views on marriage.
daily.example: Whatever it was like before, choosing not to marry isn't unusual today.

work.title: A boss's lecture
work.description: A boss scolds a veteran employee for a basic mistake.
work.example: A newcomer would be one thing, but you, in your tenth year here, making a mistake like this?

etymology: 「いざ」 is an old interjection like “well now”, and 「知らず」 is the classical form of 「知らない」. 「いざ知らず」 originally meant “well, I wouldn't know about that”, which came to mean “leaving ... aside, ... is another matter”.

similar.title: 〜ならともかく
similar.explanation: The meaning is basically the same, “…is another matter.” 〜ならともかく works in speech and writing and is the most common; 〜ならいざしらず is more literary, with a classical flavor.

similar.title: 〜ならまだしも
similar.explanation: 〜ならまだしも stresses that the first part is “milder and still barely acceptable,” with a sense of comparison; 〜ならいざしらず stresses that the first part is “another matter, outside the discussion,” and is usually a special or extreme case.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: 〜は別として also means “…is another matter,” but the tone is neutral and may simply exclude one item (「冗談は別として」). With 〜はいざしらず, the second part mostly carries criticism or a strong assertion.

formation: Built from 「なら／は」 (introducing a hypothesis or topic) + the classical interjection 「いざ」 (“well now”) + 「知らず」 (the classical negative of 「知らない」). 「いざ知らず」 originally means “well, I wouldn't know about that,” pushing the first part outside the scope of what one will address. The sentence first “sets aside” a special or understandable case, then focuses on the second part, producing the contrast “A is another matter, but B…”. Since the first part is the excluded exception, the second part is what the speaker really wants to criticize or stress.

meaning: If it were ..., it would be more or less acceptable, but the actual situation is worse and can't be tolerated.
connection: Noun / plain form + ならまだしも; noun + はまだしも

senses.label: ... would be OK, but
senses.meaning: “If it were ..., that would be understandable, but ...”. The first part is a milder, tolerable case; the second is a worse reality that can't be accepted. The second half usually shows dissatisfaction or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form + ならまだしも. Common: 「一度ならまだしも」, 「少しならまだしも」
examples: Once would be OK, but making the same mistake again and again is a problem.
Being a little late would be one thing, but not showing up without even calling is terrible.
A child would be one thing, but an adult making an excuse like that?

senses.label: ... is OK, but
senses.meaning: 「〜はまだしも」 means “... is acceptable, but ...”. It compares two things: the first is acceptable, the second isn't.
senses.connection: Noun + はまだしも
examples: The taste is OK, but this price is a bit too high.
Rain is fine, but if it snows the trains will stop.

notes: The first part must be the “milder, acceptable” side; reversing it makes no sense: ✕「何度もならまだしも、一度のミスも許せない」→ ○「一度ならまだしも、何度も同じミスをするのは困る」.
The second part is dissatisfaction, criticism, or trouble; it cannot be positive.
Saying 「〜ならまだしも」 to a client or superior carries clear blame and sounds rude.

daily.title: Complaining about neighbors
daily.description: Complaining to family about neighbors being noisy late at night.
daily.example: Daytime would be one thing, but I wish they'd stop making loud noises in the middle of the night.

daily.title: Reviewing a restaurant
daily.description: Talking with a friend about a restaurant you just tried.
daily.example: Slow food I can live with, but the staff's attitude is way too rude.

work.title: Criticizing a subordinate
work.description: A boss is unhappy with the quality of a report.
work.example: Typos are one thing, but mistakes in the numbers are unacceptable.

etymology: 「まだ」 means “still”, and 「しも」 is an old emphatic particle. 「まだしも」 means “still (relatively) better”, so 「〜ならまだしも」 is “if it were ..., that would still be better”.

similar.title: 〜ならともかく
similar.explanation: 〜ならともかく means “…aside,” excluding the first part from discussion; 〜ならまだしも stresses that the first part is “still tolerable,” with a stronger sense of comparing it to the second part.

similar.title: 〜ならいざしらず／〜はいざしらず
similar.explanation: 〜ならいざしらず is more literary and archaic, and the first part is usually a special or extreme case (「神様ならいざしらず」); 〜ならまだしも is more colloquial, and the first part is usually a milder case.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: 〜はともかく also means “leaving aside…”, and can neutrally change the subject (「味はともかく、量は多い」). 〜はまだしも carries the dissatisfaction of “the first part is tolerable, the second is not.”

formation: Built from 「なら／は」 + the adverb 「まだ」 (still, even so) + the classical emphatic particle 「しも」. 「まだしも」 itself means “(compared with other things) at least somewhat better,” so 「Aならまだしも」 means “if it were A, it would still be barely tolerable.” Using “A is acceptable” as the baseline, the sentence quietly compares B with A: B is worse than A, which creates the dissatisfaction of “A would be one thing, but B is too much.” So the first part is always the milder case, and the second part is the heavier reality that cannot be accepted.

meaning: Something (usually bad) can't be ruled out, so you should be careful or prepared.
connection: Verb nai-form / noun + でない + ないとも限らない

senses.label: Can't rule out that ...
senses.meaning: “It's not impossible that ...”, “... might happen”. The chance is small but not zero, so it's wise to prepare. The second half often brings a precaution, like 「〜から、〜ておこう」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ないとも限らない／ないとも限りません. Often with 「〜から」 or 「念のため」
examples: An earthquake could happen, so let's buy some water.
Someone might overhear us, so let's not talk about that here.
What he says might not be wrong, you know.

notes: The first part must be in the negative; dropping 「ない」 reverses the meaning completely. 「地震が起きるとも限らない」 means “it won't necessarily happen,” while 「地震が起きないとも限らない」 means “it might well happen.”
Difference from 「〜かねない」: 「かねない」 means an action may well lead to a bad result (「事故を起こしかねない」); when you only mean “the possibility can't be ruled out,” use 「〜ないとも限らない」.
Nouns and na-adjectives become 「でない」: ✕「犯人ないとも限らない」→ ○「犯人でないとも限らない」.

daily.title: Before going out
daily.description: A mother reminds her child to take an umbrella.
daily.example: It might rain, so take an umbrella.

daily.title: Keeping valuables safe
daily.description: A friend warns you to watch your wallet on a trip.
daily.example: You might run into pickpockets, so be careful with your wallet.

work.title: Risk management
work.description: Reminding everyone in a meeting to back up data.
work.example: A system failure can't be ruled out, so please be sure to make backups.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」 + 「とも」 + 「限らない」. 「限らない」 means “not necessarily”, so the literal meaning is “it's not necessarily the case that ... won't happen”: a double negative expressing possibility.

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「限らない」. 〜とは限らない follows an affirmative and means “not necessarily…”, used to deny a common belief (「高いものがいいとは限らない」); 〜ないとも限らない follows a negative and means “can't rule out that…”, used to point out a possibility.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 〜かもしれない is an ordinary conjecture, “maybe…”. 〜ないとも限らない uses a double negative to stress “can't be ruled out,” is more indirect and more literary, and often leads into precautions.

similar.title: 〜かねない
similar.explanation: 〜かねない means “may well lead to (a bad result)”; the possibility is higher and it mostly refers to consequences of an action. 〜ないとも限らない has a lower possibility; it only means it can't be ruled out.

similar.title: 〜おそれがある
similar.explanation: 〜おそれがある means “there is a risk of…” and is mostly used for objective warnings in news and notices (「津波のおそれがある」). 〜ないとも限らない is more subjective, mostly used when the speaker warns themselves or others to be careful.

formation: Built from the ない form of a verb (「起きない」) + 「とも」 (“also…”) + 「限らない」 (“not necessarily”), a double negative. The judgment 「起きない」 “is not necessarily true,” which conversely means “it may happen.” Because two negations are needed to reach “possible,” the tone is more cautious and indirect than 「起きるかもしれない」, stressing that the possibility cannot be ruled out. And because it speaks of “what if,” it often leads into precautions such as 「〜ておこう」 or 「念のため」.

meaning: Logically, doing so would be natural and appropriate. Often used when the speaker argues that something ought to be the case.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / na-adjective or noun で + しかるべきだ

senses.label: Ought to ...
senses.meaning: “Ought to ...”, “It's only right that ...”. The speaker feels that common sense or reason says it should be so, but reality often falls short, so it often sounds dissatisfied or insistent.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + しかるべきだ／しかるべきである. Common: 「認められてしかるべき」, 「謝罪があってしかるべき」
examples: His achievements deserve more recognition.
After damage on this scale, the company owes us an apology.
Public opinion ought to be reflected in policy.

senses.label: ... that ought to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜てしかるべき + noun」 modifies a noun: “a ... that ought to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + しかるべき + noun
examples: This is behavior that deserves to be punished.

notes: It needs a te-form before it, otherwise the meaning differs: 「しかるべき措置」 alone means “appropriate measures,” while 「措置がとられてしかるべきだ」 means “measures ought to be taken.”
Using it to demand that others do things for you sounds very blunt: ✕ to a superior 「私の意見も聞いてしかるべきです」→ ○「私の意見もお聞きいただけないでしょうか」.
「しかるべき」 has nothing to do with the verb 「叱る（しかる, to scold）」; do not read it as “should be scolded.”

daily.title: Giving your opinion on the news
daily.description: Discussing a company scandal with family.
daily.example: I think the person in charge ought to explain things properly.

daily.title: Standing up for a friend
daily.description: A friend's hard work isn't being recognized.
daily.example: You worked so hard; you deserve way more recognition.

work.title: Speaking up in a meeting
work.description: Arguing in a meeting for better treatment of staff.
work.example: Considering his many years of contributions, his promotion ought to be considered.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial makes demands of the government.
work.example: The government ought to take swift measures on this issue.

etymology: 「しかる」 (written 「然る」) comes from 「しか（然）＋ある」 and means “to be so, to be like that”. 「しかるべき」 is “as it should be”, which came to mean “natural, appropriate”.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 〜べきだ is an ordinary “should,” usable for advice and duty (「早く謝るべきだ」); 〜てしかるべきだ is more literary, stresses “only natural by reason,” and often contains dissatisfaction with the present state of affairs.

similar.title: 〜て当然だ
similar.explanation: 〜て当然だ is a more colloquial “it's only natural that…” and can be used for things that have already happened (「怒られて当然だ」). 〜てしかるべきだ is more formal and mostly used to assert that “it should be so (but isn't).”

similar.title: 〜ものだ（emotion, naturalness, reminiscence）
similar.explanation: 〜ものだ (in the sense of “natural”) expresses that things should generally be so by social common sense (「人に会ったら挨拶するものだ」). 〜てしかるべきだ stresses the speaker's own assertion about a specific matter.

formation: Built from a te-form + 「しかるべき」. 「しかる（然る）」 comes from 「しか（然: thus）＋あり」, meaning “to be so”; 「べき」 is the adnominal form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」, expressing “naturally, ought to.” So 「しかるべき」 means “as it should be.” With a te-form in front (「評価されて」), it becomes “being in a state of being evaluated is only natural.” Because it stresses “by rights it ought to be so,” it often implies that reality is not that way, which gives it a tone of dissatisfaction and assertion.

meaning: Because it is ... (so please forgive me / so it can't be helped). Mostly used to apologize, ask for understanding, or explain an unavoidable reason.
connection: Noun + の + こととて; verb/adjective plain form + こととて

senses.label: Because ... (apology)
senses.meaning: “Since it's ..., ...”, giving a reason and asking the listener to understand. The second half is usually an apology or an admission that you fell short. The tone is formal and old-fashioned.
senses.connection: Noun + の + こととて; verb plain form + こととて. Common: 「不慣れなこととて」, 「急なこととて」, 「子どものしたこととて」
examples: As I'm still unfamiliar with things, I sincerely apologize for the trouble I caused.
It was only a child's doing, so please forgive him.
As it was so sudden, I'm sorry I couldn't properly host you.

senses.label: Because ... (unavoidable)
senses.meaning: Because of some circumstance, the result in the second half couldn't be helped. Often follows words about a time or state.
senses.connection: Noun + の + こととて; 「〜ない／〜ぬ + こととて」
examples: It being a holiday, the government office was closed.
I didn't know, and I deeply apologize for my rudeness.

notes: It is used to explain circumstances on your own side and ask for understanding; it cannot be used to blame the other party: ✕「あなたが遅れたこととて、会議が始められなかった」→ ○「あなたが遅れたせいで…」.
Do not confuse it with 「とて」 (“even if”), which means the opposite: 「子どもとて許されない」 means “even a child can't be forgiven,” while 「子どものこととて、お許しください」 means “he's only a child, so please forgive him.”
After a noun, 「の」 is required: ✕「休日こととて」→ ○「休日のこととて」.
The second part generally does not take commands or intentions; only fixed requests for forgiveness such as 「どうかお許しください」 are possible.

daily.title: Reading a historical novel
daily.description: A character formally apologizes to an elder.
daily.example: Being young and inexperienced, I humbly ask your pardon.

daily.title: Apologizing to neighbors
daily.description: A family who just moved in formally apologizes to the neighbors.
daily.example: As we've only just moved in, we're sorry for being late to introduce ourselves.

work.title: Business apology letter
work.description: A new account manager apologizes to a client in a letter.
work.example: As I have only recently taken over, I apologize for any shortcomings.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「こと」 plus the classical particle 「とて」. 「とて」 comes from 「と＋して」 and could express a reason in Classical Japanese, so 「〜こととて」 means “since it is a matter of ...”.

similar.title: 〜とて
similar.explanation: Same origin: both contain the classical particle 「とて」. Standing alone, 〜とて usually expresses concession, “even if…” (「子どもとて容赦しない」); 〜こととて expresses a cause, used in apologies and explanations.

similar.title: 〜もので
similar.explanation: 〜もので is a colloquial way to explain a reason as an excuse (「道が混んでいたもので」). 〜こととて is more formal and archaic, mostly used in formal apologies and letters.

similar.title: 〜ゆえ（に）
similar.explanation: 〜ゆえ（に） is a general written way to give a reason, with no emotional coloring. 〜こととて carries a tone of asking the other party's understanding.

formation: Built from the formal noun 「こと」 + the classical particle 「とて」. 「とて」 is generally thought to derive from 「と＋して」, and in classical Japanese it can mean “because it is…”. 「こと」 sums up the first part as “a matter of…”, and 「とて」 then offers that matter as the reason, so the whole means “since it is that kind of matter.” By presenting the cause as an objective “matter” (「不慣れなこと」「急なこと」) rather than stressing one's own subjective reasons, it sounds humble and formal, which is why it is often used in apologies and requests for understanding.

meaning: Without doing the first thing, the second can't happen. It can also mean doing the second thing without doing the first.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなしに（は）

senses.label: Can't ... without ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ことなしに（は）〜ない」 means “can't ... without ...”, stressing that the first part is a necessary condition for the second. Similar to 「〜ないで〜することはできない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなしに（は） + 〜できない／〜ない
examples: You can't succeed without making an effort.
Without experiencing failure, people don't grow.
This plan can't move forward without the residents' understanding.

senses.label: Without ...
senses.meaning: “Without doing ..., did ...”: doing the second action without having done the first. Similar to 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ずに」, and more formal than 「〜ことなく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ことなしに + action
examples: He quit the company without consulting anyone.

notes: Whether the second part is negative changes the meaning: 「相談することなしに決めた」 means “decided without consulting,” while 「相談することなしには決められない」 means “can't decide without consulting.”
It takes only the dictionary form of verbs; for nouns use 「なくして」: ✕「努力ことなしに」→ ○「努力することなしに」「努力なくして」.
For “keep doing without…”, 「ことなく」 is generally more natural (「休むことなく働く」); use 「ことなしには」 to express a necessary condition.

daily.title: Reading an inspirational article
daily.description: An article about how to study.
daily.example: Without practicing every day, you can't hope to improve.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character quietly leaving.
daily.example: She left the town without saying goodbye.

work.title: Management policy
work.description: The company president stresses the need for reform in a speech.
work.example: I want us to keep taking on new challenges without fearing change.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper explains the preconditions for a study.
work.example: Without collecting enough data, you can't reach accurate conclusions.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「こと」 plus 「なし（無し）」 and the particle 「に」. Literally “in a state of not having done ...”. 「なし」 is the final form of the classical adjective 「無し」.

similar.title: 〜ことなく
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「こと＋無し」. 〜ことなく mainly means “without doing…” (「休むことなく働く」); 〜ことなしに is more often used for the necessary condition “can't… without…”.

similar.title: 〜なくして（は）
similar.explanation: 〜なくして follows a noun (「努力なくして成功はない」); 〜ことなしに follows the dictionary form of a verb. Both mean “without…, can't…” and both are written forms.

similar.title: 〜ないことには
similar.explanation: 〜ないことには is a more colloquial “unless one…, one can't…” (「行ってみないことには分からない」); 〜ことなしには is more literary and formal.

formation: Built from the dictionary form of a verb + the formal noun 「こと」 + 「なし」, the final form of the classical adjective 「無し」, + the case particle 「に」. 「こと」 turns the action into a noun, 「なし」 means “absence,” and 「に」 marks a state, so the whole means “in a state without the act of…”. If the second part is negative or impossible (「〜できない」), it becomes a necessary condition, “without A, B doesn't hold” → “can't B unless A”; if the second part is an ordinary action, it simply describes “doing B without A.” With 「は」 added to form 「ことなしには」, the case “without A” is picked out for contrast, strengthening the sense of “only with A will it work.”
